summary: A discussion of how to make connections between minicomputer-based terminals and a TIP more reliable. The existing protocol sends one character at a time with no error control, assuming a human can spot errors. That assumption fails for faster or automated terminals, so the author raises ways to detect and correct errors.

plainLanguage.summary: A person can notice a typo when reading, but a machine cannot. This note says the connection needs a way to check for mistakes, because no human will spot them.

subtitle: Adding error detection to terminal connections.

tldr.problem: The TIP-terminal protocol assumes a human user reads output and spots errors, but automated terminals, high-speed connections, and remote machines cannot rely on human error detection.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 230 proposes adding block-oriented data transmission and error control on top of the existing character-oriented protocol.
tldr.outcome: Error detection can be implemented at the TIP or at the serving host, improving reliability for non-interactive terminals.

facts.label: Low-speed error rate
facts.value: 1 error in 10^4 characters or better on 77.6% of calls

facts.label: Medium-speed error rate
facts.value: 1 error in 10^5 bits or better on 82% of calls

today: RFC 230 documents an early recognition that network protocol assumptions built for interactive use fail when machines communicate directly. It reflects foundational thinking about reliability in network communication.

sections.title: The Problem with Current Protocols
sections.content:
RFC 230 addresses a gap in the TIP-terminal communication protocol. The existing protocol is character-oriented with no error control, designed under the assumption that terminals would be interactive and used in character-by-character mode by humans who would detect errors through direct observation.

This assumption fails in several cases: terminals at high data rates (1200 bps or higher) where humans cannot read carefully enough, remote terminals over noisy lines with higher error rates, terminals with substantial embedded logic where no human is in the loop, and automated terminals like those for process control or remote batch entry where no human monitors the connection at all.
sections.plainLanguage: The original system was designed for a person watching data appear on their screen. But when machines talk to machines, or when data arrives too fast for anyone to read, mistakes slip through.

sections.title: Block Transmission and Error Control
sections.content:
RFC 230 proposes adding block-oriented data transmission and error control capabilities to the existing character-oriented protocol. Data blocks would include error control and block delimiting information, and would be multiples of a single character in length.

The communication channel would still transmit start and stop bits for each character, so the channel would not be as fully utilized as synchronous block communication, but the loss is not substantial. This approach allows error control to be superimposed on the existing TIP-terminal protocol without fundamentally replacing it.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of sending characters one by one with no checking, you bundle characters into blocks and add a check number so the receiver knows if something got scrambled.

sections.title: Implementation Locations
sections.content:
RFC 230 identifies two ways to implement the error control protocol. First, the control loop could terminate in the TIP itself, providing error control where it is most needed between the TIP and the terminal. However, this requires additional TIP software and block buffering capability that may overload the TIP.

Alternatively, the error control loop could end in the serving host system, either in application software or system support software. If the loop is at the host, the same software could potentially be used for host-to-host end-to-end error control in addition to host-terminal control, though with slight efficiency loss due to the embedded character-oriented format.
sections.plainLanguage: The checking can happen at the small machine (TIP) where the terminal plugs in, or at the bigger computer that the terminal is trying to reach. Each has tradeoffs.

references.text: RFC 203, Considerations for Transmission Control Protocol.
